docs.title: ⚖️ The Full-Stack Symmetry: Software & Hardware Working Together
docs.text:
Autonomous machinery requires simultaneous mastery of the mind (firmware) and the muscles (circuits). Every unit in this curriculum is built with symmetrical software and hardware counterparts:

Unit Track 1: Embedded Rust (Mind) Track 2: Embedded Hardware (Muscles) Unit 1 Syntax, Fixed-Width Ints, RAM Physics, AOT Compilation Circuit Physics, Ohm's Law, Passives (R, C, L), Diodes Unit 2 Ownership, Move Semantics, Borrowing, Lifetimes Power Trees, Battery Chemistries, LDOs, Buck Converters, BMS Unit 3 Structs, Enums, Pattern Matching, Typestates Transistors, Logic-Level MOSFETs, H-Bridges, Motor Drivers Unit 4 Zero-Cost Abstractions, Traits, Driver Crates Sensor Physics, Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps), Filters, IMUs Unit 5 Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO), Registers, Bitmasking Wire-Level Communication Buses (GPIO, I2C, SPI, UART, OLED) Unit 6 Async Embassy, Real-Time RTOS, Concurrency Noise, Ground Loops, EMC, Schematics, Multimeters, KiCad PCBs

docs.title: 🛡️ NASA Power of 10: Rules for Safety-Critical Systems
docs.text: [!IMPORTANT] The Golden Safety Standard for Robotics & Drones The Power of 10 rules were originally authored by Gerard J. Holzmann at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) to program deep-space probes and Mars rovers. In autonomous robotics, a crash is not an error log—it is physical damage or personal injury.

docs.title: 1. Eliminate All Recursion
docs.text:
• Rule: Never write a function that calls itself.
  • Silicon Reality: Microcontrollers operate with constrained stack memory (e.g., 32 KB to 264 KB). Unbounded recursion or unexpected sensor values can cause stack overflow into data memory, causing hard faults. Use iterative loops (for / while) with fixed bounds.

docs.title: 2. Guarantee Fixed Upper Bounds on All Loops
docs.text:
• Rule: Every loop must have an absolute maximum upper limit of iterations.
  • Silicon Reality: Control loops must meet strict real-time deadlines (e.g. 1 kHz PID loops). Never write while !sensor_ready(). Always bound waiting loops with MAX_RETRIES or .take(N).

docs.title: 3. Ban Dynamic Heap Allocation After Boot (#![no_std] + heapless)
docs.text:
• Rule: Zero dynamic memory allocation (malloc, Vec, String) during operational control.
  • Silicon Reality: Dynamic allocation causes heap fragmentation. In embedded systems lacking virtual memory, fragmentation eventually triggers allocation failure panics. Pre-allocate all queues and buffers statically using fixed-capacity types (heapless::Vec).

docs.title: 4. Keep Functions Modular and Under 60 Lines
docs.text:
• Rule: Every function must fit within 60 lines of code.
  • Silicon Reality: Single-purpose, modular functions fit completely on a screen, preventing cognitive overload and making formal verification straightforward.

docs.title: 5. Zero Panics — Treat Panicking Code as a Compilation Bug
docs.text:
• Rule: Production firmware must be mathematically proven never to invoke panic handlers.
  • Silicon Reality: A panic halts the CPU and drops PWM signals, causing robots to stall or drones to crash. Never use .unwrap(), .expect(), or direct unchecked slice indexing (data[i]). Use data.get(i) and Option/Result.

docs.title: 6. Minimize Variable Scopes and Enforce Immutability
docs.text:
• Rule: Variables must default to immutable (let), kept within the narrowest practical scope.
  • Silicon Reality: Restricting mutation prevents accidental state corruption across concurrent tasks and interrupts.

docs.title: 7. Zero Unchecked Returns (#![deny(unused_must_use)])
docs.text:
• Rule: Explicitly inspect and handle every return value.
  • Silicon Reality: Ignoring a hardware bus error (e.g. I2C NACK) means operating on garbage data. Enforce #![deny(unused_must_use)] and propagate errors with the ? operator.

docs.title: 8. Restrict Macro Metaprogramming in Safety Paths
docs.text:
• Rule: Avoid procedural macros or opaque macro loops in real-time control paths.
  • Silicon Reality: Safety loops require transparent, easily auditable assembly code. Prefer plain functions, const fn, and traits over macro magic.

docs.title: 9. Pure Safe Rust Only (#![forbid(unsafe_code)])
docs.text:
• Rule: Ban unsafe blocks from high-level robotic application logic.
  • Silicon Reality: Isolate raw register accesses inside verified Hardware Abstraction Layers (HALs). Robot decision code, FSMs, and navigation logic must run in 100% verified Safe Rust.

docs.title: 10. Enforce Zero-Warning Compilation and Formal Verification
docs.text:
• Rule: Zero compiler warnings tolerated; verify safety via Clippy, Miri, and formal verifiers (Kani).
  • Silicon Reality: Warnings signal latent bugs. Compile with #![deny(warnings)] and #![warn(clippy::pedantic)].

docs.title: Safety-Critical Starter Template
docs.text:
#![no_std]                 // Rule 3: No dynamic heap runtime
#![no_main]                // Standard: Baremetal reset vector boot
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]    // Rule 9: 100% Safe Rust in application logic
#![deny(warnings)]         // Rule 10: Zero compiler warnings tolerated
#![deny(unused_must_use)]  // Rule 7: Every Result and error handled
#![warn(clippy::pedantic)] // Rule 10: Strict linter checks

use core::panic::PanicInfo;

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(_info: &PanicInfo) -> ! {
    // 1. Cut power to all actuator PWM lines immediately (safe shutdown)
    // 2. Set fault status LED to solid red
    // 3. Enter infinite halt loop or trigger watchdog hardware reset
    loop {}
}

docs.title: ⚡ Track 2: Embedded Hardware & Robotics Design Syllabus
Unit 1: Foundations of Circuit Physics & Passive Components
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: The Silicon Ground Truth: Voltage, Current, Resistance & Power
  • Electron drift velocity vs. electromagnetic wave propagation across copper traces.
  • Ohm’s Law (\(V = IR\)), Kirchhoff’s Current & Voltage Laws (KCL, KVL).
  • Electrical Power & Joule’s Heating (\(P = VI = I^2 R\)): Thermal limits of tiny components.
  • Conductors, Insulators, and Semiconductor Bandgaps (Silicon vs. Gallium Nitride).
  • Chapter 2: Resistor Architecture & Voltage Slicing
  • Resistor technologies: Thin-film, thick-film, carbon, and parasitic inductance.
  • Precise Voltage Dividers: The Loading Effect (\(R_{\text{load}} \parallel R_2\)) and input impedance.
  • Sizing Pull-Up and Pull-Down Resistors: Balancing rise-time (\(\tau = RC\)) against current consumption.
  • Chapter 3: Capacitors: Electric Fields, Dielectrics & Power Stabilization
  • Physics of capacitance (\(C = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}\)) and dielectric polarization.
  • Ceramic (MLCC) vs. Tantalum vs. Aluminum Electrolytic vs. Polymer capacitors.
  • The DC Bias Trap: Why a 10µF ceramic cap drops to 2µF at rated operating voltage.
  • Equivalent Series Resistance (ESR) and Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL).
  • Chapter 4: Inductors, Magnetic Coils & The Inductive Kickback Trap
  • Magnetic flux, Faraday’s Law, Lenz’s Law, and back-EMF (\(V = -L \frac{di}{dt}\)).
  • Why cutting power to a motor generates a negative 100V spike that destroys microcontrollers.
  • Core saturation, hysteresis losses, and toroidal vs. drum inductors.
  • Chapter 5: Semiconductor Physics: Diodes & Voltage Clamping
  • The P-N junction, barrier potential, and forward voltage drop (\(V_f\)).
  • Standard Silicon vs. Schottky Diodes (low \(V_f \approx 0.2\text{V}\), nanosecond recovery).
  • Zener Diodes (voltage regulation) and TVS Diodes (Electrostatic Discharge / ESD clamping).
  • The Flyback / Freewheeling Diode: Sizing current rating and reverse recovery time.

docs.title: Unit 2: Power Trees, Battery Management & Voltage Regulation
docs.text:
• Chapter 6: Power Tree Architecture for Robotics
  • Designing multi-rail power distribution (e.g. 14.8V LiPo \(\rightarrow\) 12V Motors \(\rightarrow\) 5V Servos \(\rightarrow\) 3.3V MCU).
  • Inrush current, soft-start circuits, reverse polarity protection, and fuse sizing.
  • Chapter 7: Linear Voltage Regulators (LDOs)
  • Internal topology: Bandgap voltage reference, error amplifier, and pass transistor (NPN vs. P-MOSFET).
  • Dropout voltage (\(V_{\text{drop}}\)), thermal dissipation (\(P = (V_{\text{in}} - V_{\text{out}}) \times I\)), and thermal runaway.
  • Output capacitor ESR stability requirements (preventing LDO feedback oscillation).
  • Chapter 8: Switching Regulators (Buck, Boost & Buck-Boost)
  • High-efficiency DC-DC conversion: Inductor energy storage cycle.
  • Step-Down (Buck) topology: Duty cycle equations (\(V_{\text{out}} = D \times V_{\text{in}}\)).
  • Step-Up (Boost) topology for battery-powered stepping.
  • Switching frequency tradeoffs (100 kHz vs. 2 MHz): Ripple voltage vs. magnetic coil volume.
  • Chapter 9: Battery Chemistry, Charging & Battery Management Systems (BMS)
  • LiPo (Lithium Polymer) vs. 18650 Li-ion vs. LiFePO4: Nominal, fully charged, and cutoff voltages.
  • C-Ratings (Continuous vs. Burst discharge) and internal resistance (\(R_{\text{int}}\)) voltage sag under motor load.
  • Cell balancing (Passive vs. Active) and Over-Voltage / Under-Voltage / Over-Current cutoff circuits.
  • Chapter 10: Circuit Protection & Reverse Polarity Architecture
  • Diode protection (and why it wastes too much power at high currents).
  • High-side P-Channel MOSFET reverse polarity protection circuits.
  • Ideal Diode Controllers: Zero-voltage-drop active rectification.

docs.title: Unit 3: Transistors, Power Switching & Actuator Drivers
docs.text:
• Chapter 11: Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT: NPN & PNP)
  • Current-controlled current source: Base current (\(I_B\)), Collector current (\(I_C\)), and Gain (\(\beta / h_{FE}\)).
  • Saturation vs. Cutoff modes: Sizing base resistors for clean digital switching.
  • Chapter 12: MOSFETs: The Workhorses of Modern Robotics
  • N-Channel vs. P-Channel: Voltage-controlled field-effect switching.
  • Gate threshold voltage (\(V_{GS(\text{th})}\)): Why "Logic-Level" MOSFETs are mandatory for 3.3V microcontrollers.
  • On-Resistance (\(R_{DS(\text{on})}\)), gate capacitance (\(C_{\text{iss}}\)), and gate charge (\(Q_g\)).
  • Gate Driver ICs: Supplying high-current pulses to switch MOSFET gates in nanoseconds.
  • Chapter 13: Brushed DC Motors & H-Bridge Topologies
  • Motor electrical model: Armature resistance (\(R\)), inductance (\(L\)), and Back-EMF constant (\(K_v\)).
  • The 4-Switch H-Bridge: Shoot-through danger and dead-time insertion.
  • Driver ICs: DRV8833, TB6612FNG, and high-current discrete MOSFET H-bridges.
  • Chapter 14: Servo Motors & Stepper Motor Drive Circuits
  • RC Hobby Servos: Internal feedback potentiometer, 50 Hz PWM timing, and torque sizing.
  • Bipolar Stepper Motors: Microstepping current chopping, A4988 vs. TMC2209 silent drivers.
  • Chapter 15: Brushless DC Motors (BLDC) & 3-Phase Inverters
  • 3-Phase stator coils and permanent magnet rotors.
  • Sensored (Hall-effect) vs. Sensorless (Back-EMF zero-crossing detection).
  • Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) architecture: 6-MOSFET bridge, gate drivers, DShot digital protocol.

docs.title: Unit 4: Sensor Physics, Analog Signal Conditioning & Op-Amps
docs.text:
• Chapter 16: Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps) in Robotics
  • The Ideal Op-Amp model: Infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, virtual short.
  • Voltage Follower / Buffer: Isolating high-impedance sensors from ADC loading.
  • Inverting and Non-Inverting Amplifiers: Sizing gain for weak analog sensors.
  • Differential Amplifiers & Current Shunt Sensing: Measuring high-side motor current.
  • Chapter 17: Analog Filters & Signal Conditioning
  • Passive RC Low-Pass and High-Pass Filters: Cutoff frequency (\(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}\)).
  • Active Op-Amp Filters (Sallen-Key topology) for sharp sensor noise cutoff.
  • Anti-Aliasing Filters: Satisfying the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem before the ADC.
  • Chapter 18: Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs: Accelerometers & Gyroscopes)
  • MEMS physics: Microscopic capacitive silicon comb finger arrays.
  • Coriolis vibratory gyroscopes: Measuring angular velocity in degrees per second.
  • Noise profiles: Accelerometer vibration noise vs. Gyroscope bias drift.
  • Chapter 19: Distance, Position & Environmental Sensors
  • Time-of-Flight (ToF) Laser / LiDAR sensors (VL53L0X): Photon timing physics.
  • Ultrasonic transducers: Piezoelectric crystals, speed of sound, temperature drift.
  • Optical vs. Magnetic Hall-effect encoders: Quadrature pulse decoding (\(A/B\) channels).

docs.title: Unit 5: Physical-Layer Communication Buses & Display Hardware
docs.text:
• Chapter 20: Digital GPIO Electrical Characteristics
  • Push-Pull vs. Open-Drain / Open-Collector silicon stages.
  • Logic threshold voltages (\(V_{IH}, V_{IL}, V_{OH}, V_{OL}\)) and noise margins.
  • Slew rate control and drive strength configuration in microcontroller registers.
  • Chapter 21: The I2C Physical Layer (Inter-Integrated Circuit)
  • Open-drain bus architecture: Why pull-up resistors are physically required on SDA and SCL.
  • Bus Capacitance limits (400 pF standard) and rise-time calculations.
  • Multi-master arbitration, clock stretching, and addressing collisions.
  • Chapter 22: The SPI Physical Layer (Serial Peripheral Interface)
  • Synchronous push-pull signaling: High-speed clock lines (up to 50+ MHz).
  • Transmission line reflections, signal termination resistors, and line length limits.
  • Multi-slave configurations: Individual Chip Selects (CS) vs. Daisy-chaining.
  • Chapter 23: UART, Asynchronous Serial & Differential Signaling
  • Baud rate generators, bit timing sampling (16x oversampling), and clock drift tolerances.
  • Logic levels: TTL (0V–3.3V) vs. RS-232 (\(\pm 12\text{V}\)) vs. Differential RS-485.
  • Chapter 24: Visual Displays & Frame Buffer Hardware
  • 0.96" OLED displays (SSD1306): Charge pumps (generating 7–10V on-chip), column/page addressing.
  • TFT LCDs (ST7789, ILI9341): Parallel vs. SPI, backlight LED current driver circuits.

docs.title: Unit 6: Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC), Schematics & Lab Tools
docs.text:
• Chapter 25: Noise, Ground Loops & Decoupling Architecture
  • The physics of Ground: Ground loops, return current paths, and star-ground topologies.
  • Decoupling capacitor placement: Loop inductance and why capacitor distance from pins matters.
  • Analog Ground (AGND) vs. Digital Ground (DGND) on mixed-signal microcontrollers.
  • Chapter 26: Reading Schematics & Component Datasheets Like an Architect
  • Decoding pin multiplexing tables, truth tables, and bus timing diagrams.
  • Interpreting "Absolute Maximum Ratings" vs. "Recommended Operating Conditions".
  • Understanding schematic net labels, power symbols, and bill-of-materials (BOM).
  • Chapter 27: The Hardware Lab Bench & Test Instruments
  • Digital Multimeter (DMM): Measuring voltage, continuity, and measuring current without blowing fuses.
  • The USB Logic Analyzer & PulseView: Sniffing real I2C, SPI, and PWM pulses on your Linux PC.
  • Basic Oscilloscopes: Reading analog waveforms, noise spikes, and voltage ripple.
  • Chapter 28: Prototyping to Production: Breadboards, Perfboards & PCB Design
  • Breadboard limitations: Parasitic capacitance, loose spring contacts, and current limits (<1A).
  • Stripboards & Perfboards: Reliable soldered prototypes.
  • Introduction to KiCad: Schematic capture, PCB footprint assignment, trace routing, and Gerber generation.

docs.title: NASA Power of 10: Rules for Safety-Critical Systems
docs.text:
[!IMPORTANT] The Golden Safety Standard for Robotics & Drones The Power of 10 rules were originally created by Gerard J. Holzmann at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) to write code for spacecraft and Mars rovers.

In a spacecraft or a flying drone, you cannot press Ctrl+C to restart the program if it crashes. If your software freezes, panics, or runs out of memory, physical hardware breaks.

Below are the 10 Golden Rules adapted specifically for Embedded Rust, explaining why each rule exists and how to follow it in simple words.

docs.title: 1. Eliminate All Recursion
docs.text:
• The Rule: Never write a function that calls itself.
  • Why this matters on hardware: Microcontrollers have very tiny memory (RAM), often only 32 KB to 256 KB. Every time a function calls itself, it consumes another chunk of stack memory. If recursion goes too deep—or loops infinitely because a sensor gave an unexpected reading—the stack overflows, crashes into your program data, and reboots or freezes the chip mid-flight.
  • In simple words: Replace all tree-walks, graph searches, and repeated calculations with standard iterative loops (for or while) using a fixed counter.

docs.title: 2. Guarantee Fixed Upper Bounds on All Loops
docs.text:
• The Rule: Every loop must have an absolute maximum number of times it can repeat.
  • Why this matters on hardware: A balancing robot or drone must check sensors and adjust motors at a precise frequency (e.g., 1,000 times every second). If a loop hangs waiting for a slow sensor or broken wire, the motor controls freeze and the robot loses balance.
  • In simple words: Never write an unbounded while !sensor_ready() loop. Always write: 
    // Safe bounded loop: try at most 100 times, then time out
for _ in 0..MAX_RETRIES {
    if sensor.is_ready() {
        break;
    }
}
    Or use the .take(N) iterator adapter on streams.

docs.title: 3. Ban Dynamic Heap Allocation After Boot (#![no_std] + heapless)
docs.text:
• The Rule: Never use dynamic heap memory allocators (malloc, free, standard Vec, or String) during normal operation.
  • Why this matters on hardware: On your laptop, you can ask the operating system for more RAM anytime. Microcontrollers have no OS and very little RAM. Allocating and freeing memory repeatedly creates memory fragmentation (like Swiss cheese with lots of tiny holes). Eventually, a memory allocation fails, causing an instant panic and crash.
  • In simple words:
  • Compile strictly with #![no_std].
  • Decide the maximum capacity for all queues, sensor buffers, and packet frames at compile time.
  • Use fixed-size arrays ([u8; 64]) or static crates like heapless (e.g., heapless::Vec<u8, 64>), which allocate all memory safely on the stack or in static memory once at startup.

docs.title: 4. Keep Functions Modular and Under 60 Lines
docs.text:
• The Rule: Keep every function under 60 lines of code.
  • Why this matters: A 60-line function fits on a single laptop screen without scrolling. You can easily see all inputs, internal logic, and return values at a glance.
  • In simple words: A function should do only one dedicated job. If a function is getting long or doing multiple things (like reading a sensor, calculating a PID value, and commanding a motor), break it into separate, focused helper functions.

docs.title: 5. Zero Panics — Treat Panicking Code as a Compilation Bug
docs.text:
• The Rule: A panic in production embedded code is considered a critical bug.
  • Why this matters on hardware: On a laptop, a panic displays a red error message in your terminal. On a drone flying at 30 km/h, a panic turns off the CPU, disables PWM motor signals, and sends the drone into freefall.
  • In simple words:
  • Never use standard panic!, assert!, or unchecked direct array indexing like data[i] (if i is out of bounds, Rust panics).
  • Use safe accessors like data.get(i) which returns Option<&T>.
  • Use safe math operations: .checked_add(), .saturating_add(), or .saturating_mul() so number overflows never trigger a panic.
  • Use the Typestate Pattern to ensure invalid hardware states are impossible to represent at compile time.
  • Every fallible hardware operation must return an explicit Result<T, E>.

docs.title: 6. Minimize Variable Scopes and Enforce Immutability
docs.text:
• The Rule: Variables must default to immutable (let), with variable lifespans kept as short as possible.
  • Why this matters: If a variable can be changed (mut) throughout an entire 100-line function, any line of code can accidentally overwrite critical sensor data.
  • In simple words:
  • Always use let by default.
  • Only use let mut when you genuinely need to mutate a value, and keep it confined inside the smallest possible code block { ... }.
  • Use block expressions and variable shadowing to discard intermediate calculations as soon as you are done with them.

docs.title: 7. Zero Unchecked Returns (#![deny(unused_must_use)] & No .unwrap())
docs.text:
• The Rule: You must explicitly check and handle the return value of every function.
  • Why this matters on hardware: If an I2C sensor read fails and your code ignores the returned error, your control loop acts on stale or garbage data. If you use .unwrap() and an error occurs, the chip crashes.
  • In simple words:
  • Add #![deny(unused_must_use)] at the top of your crate so the compiler refuses to compile if you ignore any Result.
  • Never use .unwrap() or .expect() in flight or robot code.
  • Always handle both outcomes explicitly using match, if let, or the question-mark ? operator.

docs.title: 8. Restrict Macro Metaprogramming in Safety Paths
docs.text:
• The Rule: Do not use complex recursive macros or procedural macros in real-time control loops.
  • Why this matters: Fancy macros hide code generation behind the scenes, making it difficult to understand what machine instructions the CPU is actually executing.
  • In simple words: Keep your code plain, readable, and predictable. Replace complex macros with standard functions, compile-time functions (const fn), and traits.

docs.title: 9. Pure Safe Rust Only (#![forbid(unsafe_code)])
docs.text:
• The Rule: Ban unsafe blocks from application, navigation, and control logic.
  • Why this matters: Safe Rust guarantees memory safety and prevents dangling pointers, buffer overflows, and data races at compile time. Using unsafe disables these guarantees.
  • In simple words:
  • Place #![forbid(unsafe_code)] at the top of your robotics control files.
  • Raw hardware access (reading/writing hardware registers via memory addresses) should only happen inside tested, certified hardware libraries (HALs and PACs).
  • Your main robot brain, state machines, and flight logic should be 100% pure Safe Rust.
  • Prefer static dispatch (generics and traits) over dynamic dispatch (&dyn Trait) to avoid slow vtable lookups and indirect function calls.

docs.title: 10. Enforce Zero-Warning Compilation and Formal Verification
docs.text:
• The Rule: Every build must compile with zero warnings, and critical algorithms should be verified with automated tools.
  • Why this matters: A compiler warning is a bug waiting to happen. In robotics, small oversights cause physical damage.
  • In simple words:
  • Treat all compiler warnings as errors by configuring workspace lints: 
    #![deny(warnings)]
#![warn(clippy::pedantic)]
#![warn(clippy::nursery)]
  • Use automated verification tools:
    • Clippy (cargo clippy): Catches non-idiomatic code, inefficient patterns, and potential bugs.
    • Kani Rust Verifier: A mathematical model-checking tool that proves your code will never panic or overflow under any possible input.
    • Miri (cargo miri): An interpreter that checks for undefined behavior, memory leaks, and alignment errors.

docs.title: The Safety-Critical Embedded Rust Starter Template
docs.text:
Putting all 10 rules together, every robust bare-metal robotics project starts with this compiler configuration at the root of main.rs:

#![no_std]                 // Rule 3: No dynamic heap OS runtime
#![no_main]                // Standard: Hardware boots directly to our entry point
#![forbid(unsafe_code)]    // Rule 9: Zero unsafe code in application logic
#![deny(warnings)]         // Rule 10: Zero compiler warnings tolerated
#![deny(unused_must_use)]  // Rule 7: Every Result and error must be checked
#![warn(clippy::pedantic)] // Rule 10: Enable the strictest linter checks

use core::panic::PanicInfo;

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(_info: &PanicInfo) -> ! {
    // In safety-critical robotics:
    // 1. Instantly cut power to all motors and actuators (failsafe).
    // 2. Set status LED to solid red.
    // 3. Halt the CPU in an infinite loop or trigger a controlled watchdog reboot.
    loop {}
}

docs.title: Chapter 1: From Java/Python to Rust: Syntax & Execution Model
1.1 The Compilation Model: Bytecode & Interpreters vs. Ahead-of-Time (AOT) Machine Code
Overview: Interpreters vs. JITs vs. Native Ahead-of-Time (AOT)
docs.text:
• Programs written in Java and Python run on top of an intermediary abstraction layer: a Virtual Machine (JVM) or an Interpreter (CPython).
  • When programming microcontrollers for robotics, this managed execution model collapses under strict hardware and timing limits. To build reliable systems, we must understand why managed runtimes fail on bare metal and how Rust's Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation delivers bare-metal control with zero overhead.

docs.title: Architectural Pipeline Comparison: Python vs. Java vs. Rust
docs.text:
Here is what happens between our source code and the physical CPU:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. PYTHON (Interpreted Bytecode Pipeline)                                   │
│                                                                             │
│   code.py ──> Bytecode (.pyc) ──> [ CPython Interpreter (in C) ] ──> CPU    │
│                                   ├── Requires Host OS & Dynamic Allocator  │
│                                   ├── Reference Counting & Cyclic GC        │
│                                   └── High Overhead (~10MB+ RAM baseline)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. JAVA (Just-In-Time Compiled Bytecode Pipeline)                           │
│                                                                             │
│   code.java ──> Bytecode (.class) ──> [ JVM (Java Virtual Machine) ] ──> CPU│
│                                       ├── JIT Warmup & Compilation Jitter   │
│                                       ├── Tracing Garbage Collector Pauses  │
│                                       └── Massive Footprint (~30MB-100MB+)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. RUST (Ahead-Of-Time Native Machine Code Pipeline)                        │
│                                                                             │
│   main.rs ──> [ rustc + LLVM ] ──> Pure Machine Code (.bin/.elf) ──> CPU    │
│               Ahead-Of-Time        ├── Zero Runtime / No Interpreter        │
│               Compilation & Safety ├── Direct Memory-Mapped I/O Registers   │
│               Checks               └── Cycle-Accurate (< 2KB RAM footprint) │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Dimension Python Java Rust Translation Interpreted Bytecode JIT-compiled Bytecode Ahead-of-Time (AOT) to Machine Code Runtime Engine CPython interpreter binary JVM (Java Virtual Machine) None (Zero runtime overhead) Memory Management Reference counting + cyclic GC Tracing Garbage Collector Compile-time Ownership (No GC) RAM Footprint Tens of megabytes (10 MB+ minimum) Hundreds of megabytes (30–64 MB+ minimum) Bytes to kilobytes (operates within < 2 KB RAM) Execution Timing Non-deterministic (slow, dynamic dispatch) Jittery (JIT compilation warm-up + GC pauses) Cycle-accurate, hard-real-time determinism

docs.title: Physical Silicon Constraints of Microcontrollers
docs.text:
Microcontrollers (such as the RP2350 on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 or an STM32H7 on a drone flight controller) typically have:

  • Flash (Code Storage): < 4 MB on-chip (up to 32 MB via external QSPI Flash)
  • RAM (Active Working Memory): 64 KB to 1.4 MB
  • Clock Speed: 48 MHz to 600 MHz

docs.title: The Triad of Failure: Why Managed Runtimes Break Bare Metal
docs.text:
1. The RAM Cliff: A standard JVM or Python interpreter binary requires tens of megabytes just to initialize its runtime engine. Its baseline memory overhead exceeds the entire physical RAM of most microcontrollers before user code even starts executing.

  2. The "Stop-the-World" Garbage Collection Problem (Fatal for Robotics):

  3. Imagine our mini-robot reads an IMU / gyroscope 1,000 times per second (1 kHz) to balance on two wheels.

  4. If a garbage collector pauses execution for even 10 milliseconds to reclaim unused memory, the control loop misses 10 consecutive sensor updates and motor corrections. The robot loses balance and crashes.

  5. Direct Silicon Access via Hardware Registers:

  6. On a microcontroller, hardware peripherals (GPIO, PWM, I2C, SPI) are controlled by reading from and writing to specific physical addresses in memory (Memory-Mapped I/O).
  7. In Rust, modifying a hardware register compiles directly into a single CPU str (store) instruction. There is no interpreter or virtual machine translating instructions or introducing latency.

[!NOTE] Ahead-of-Time (AOT) In Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation, 100% of translation, optimization, borrow checking, and type validation occurs on your host machine before the binary touches silicon. When flashing a microcontroller, you write pure machine code directly into the chip's Flash memory. The CPU begins executing instructions immediately on power-up with zero startup lag, zero runtime overhead, and cycle-accurate predictability.

docs.title: 1.2 Cargo, Toolchains, and Cross-Compilation Targets
docs.text:
In Java and Python, we rarely think about the CPU architecture of our machine. In embedded robotics, it is the very first thing we configure.

[!NOTE] What is "Embedded"? - Embedded means the computer hardware and software are permanently built inside a specific physical product (like a drone, a microwave, or a mini-robot) to do one dedicated job, rather than running on a general-purpose PC. - In simple words: Stop thinking like a desktop developer with infinite RAM, a massive operating system, and a monitor. Start thinking like an engineer working directly with voltages, hardware pins, sensors, and real-time physical limits.

[!NOTE] What is "Firmware"? - Firmware is the low-level code permanently saved inside a hardware chip's Flash memory. It gives the device its basic brain and operating logic right from the moment it gets power.

docs.title: Host vs. Target: Why We Cross-Compile
docs.text:
• Host (Your Development Machine):
  • The laptop or PC you are sitting in front of right now (e.g., your PC running Linux on a 64-bit Intel/AMD processor).

  • Has a full operating system (OS) and gigabytes of RAM.

  • Target (The Robot's Brain):

  • The actual tiny microcontroller chip inside our robot or drone (for example, an STM32F4 running an ARM Cortex-M4 processor).
  • Has no operating system (Bare Metal) and very little RAM (kilobytes).
  • Microcontrollers can be 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit, or 64-bit. For modern robotics, 32-bit is the sweet spot.

Because the target chip is too small to run a compiler by itself, our laptop (the Host) must compile machine code specifically formatted for the chip's CPU (the Target).

This process is called Cross-Compilation.

[!NOTE] What is Cross-Compilation? - Cross-compilation simply means: compiling code on Machine A (the Host) to produce an executable that runs on Machine B (the Target). - It does not mean the code runs everywhere. It produces a binary file made specifically and only for that target chip!

[!NOTE] .bin vs. .elf Files - .bin (Raw Binary): A pure list of machine code 0s and 1s that the target chip directly understands. - .elf (Executable and Linkable Format): Contains the exact same machine code 0s and 1s, PLUS extra helper information (metadata): memory addresses, function names, variable names, and debugging symbols. - How they are used: The .elf file stays on your laptop so your debugger can show function names and line numbers. When flashing, only the raw machine code goes into the chip. Using .elf is the standard and recommended way in embedded Rust.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Target Triple
docs.text:
A Target Triple is like an order form you give to the compiler.

When we tell Rust: "Hey compiler, please translate my code into machine code," the compiler needs answers to 4 specific questions: 1. Architecture: What instruction dialect does the CPU speak? 2. Vendor: Who made the chip? (Usually unknown or none) 3. OS: What operating system manages the hardware? (For bare metal, this is none) 4. Environment / ABI: What low-level calling rules must it follow?

[!NOTE] Why is it called a "Triple"? Historically it had 3 parts: arch-vendor-os. Later, people added a 4th part for the environment/ABI, but everyone still calls it a "triple"!

docs.title: Deep Dive: Decoding the ARM Drone Target (thumbv7em-none-eabihf)
docs.text: Let's break down this common drone target string: * thumbv7em — Architecture * none — Vendor * none — Operating System * eabihf — ABI / Environment

docs.title: 1. Architecture: thumbv7em (ARMv7-EM & Thumb Mode)
docs.text:
• Standard ARM processors originally used 32-bit long instructions. Later, ARM created a compressed, memory-saving instruction mode called Thumb so programs take up less Flash storage on tiny chips.
  • v7em stands for the ARMv7-EM architecture (found in chips like ARM Cortex-M4 and Cortex-M7).
  • What this tells Rust: "Only produce machine instructions that a Cortex-M4 or Cortex-M7 processor can understand."

docs.title: 2. Vendor: none (Vendor-Agnostic Silicon)
docs.text: • Hardware vendor is unassigned (the code is not tied to Apple, PC, etc., and works across chip makers).

docs.title: 3. Operating System: none (Bare Metal & #![no_std])
docs.text: This is one of the most important concepts in embedded programming: * On your laptop, the target is x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu. When your code wants to print text or allocate memory, it asks the Linux kernel to do it. * On your drone chip, there is no operating system — no Linux, no Windows, no helper software. * When our code starts running, it is in direct and total control of the hardware. This is called Bare Metal. * What this tells Rust: "Do not include any code that tries to make Linux or Windows system calls. There is no OS here to answer them!" (This is why in embedded Rust, we must add #![no_std] at the top of our program).

docs.title: 4. Environment & ABI: eabihf (Hardware Float Calling Conventions)
docs.text: Let's split eabihf into two simple parts: eabi and hf.

docs.title: Part A: What is an ABI (and EABI)?
docs.text:
• API is for humans writing code: "I call the function add(5, 10)."
  • ABI (Application Binary Interface) is the rulebook for the CPU hardware:
  • When add(5, 10) is called, does 5 go into CPU hardware register R0 or R1?
  • Does the answer 15 come back in register R0 or on the stack?
  • Once code is compiled into 0s and 1s, variable names like a and b disappear. The CPU only has physical storage slots called Registers and RAM.
  • EABI (Embedded ABI): A standard rulebook created by ARM for microcontrollers so that code written in Rust, C, or Assembly can talk to each other without mixing up CPU registers.
Source Code (API):            result = add(5, 10);
                                      │
                         Compiler applies the ABI rules
                                      ▼
Binary Machine Code (ABI):    1. LOAD 5 INTO Register R0
                              2. LOAD 10 INTO Register R1
                              3. CALL FUNCTION `add`
                              4. READ ANSWER FROM Register R0

The ABI is the rulebook that says: "Whenever any function is called on this ARM chip, parameter 1 goes to register R0, parameter 2 goes to R1, parameter 3 goes to R2, parameter 4 goes to R3. The return value comes back in R0."

If two pieces of code used different ABIs, Function A would place 5 into R0, but Function B would expect it in R1. The program would read garbage and crash immediately.

docs.title: Part B: What is Hardware Floating Point (hf)?
docs.text:
This is where the magic happens for robotics and drones!

In robotics, we constantly work with decimals (f32 in Rust), such as measuring angles: 

let angle: f32 = 45.25 * 3.14159;

How does a CPU calculate 45.25 * 3.14159? There are two completely different ways: * Software Floating Point (regular eabi without hf): The CPU has no decimal math hardware. The compiler has to run dozens of slow integer tricks to estimate the decimal. This is slow! * Hardware Floating Point (eabihf): The chip has a dedicated physical math unit called an FPU (Floating Point Unit). * The compiler generates direct FPU machine instructions (VADD, VMUL, VSQRT). * It passes our f32 numbers directly inside the chip's ultra-fast dedicated FPU registers (s0, s1). * Math finishes in a single clock cycle!

docs.title: ARM Microcontroller Target Comparison Table
docs.text: Target String Meaning in Plain English thumbv7m-none-eabi Cortex-M3: Bare-metal MCU, no hardware floating point (uses slow software math for decimals). thumbv7em-none-eabi Cortex-M4: Bare-metal MCU with FPU disabled or not present. thumbv7em-none-eabihf Cortex-M4 / M7: Bare-metal MCU with Hardware Floating Point enabled (super fast decimal math for drones, motors, and PID controllers).

docs.title: Core Silicon Principles: Architecture, Bus Width & Clock Cycles
docs.text:
[!NOTE] What is a CPU Architecture? - An architecture (Instruction Set Architecture, or ISA) is not software. It is the blueprint and dictionary of a processor. - It defines: - What physical instructions the circuitry understands (e.g., ADD, SUB, JUMP). - How many physical registers the CPU has and how wide they are. - How memory addresses work. - Think of it like spoken languages: - x86_64 is like English. - ARM (Thumb) is like Spanish. - RISC-V is like Japanese.

An ARM chip physically cannot understand an x86 instruction because its internal transistor circuits are wired completely differently.

[!NOTE] What does "32-bit" or "8-bit" mean? - It does not mean running 32 instructions at the same time! - It means: The width of the data pipes and registers inside the CPU is 32 bits wide. - In a 32-bit CPU (like Cortex-M4): - Each general register holds a 32-bit binary number (00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000). - In one clock cycle (one "tick" of electricity), the math unit can add two 32-bit numbers together (up to 4 billion!). - A memory address is 32 bits long, meaning it can address up to 4 Gigabytes of memory. - In an 8-bit CPU (like the old Arduino Uno / ATmega328P): - Registers are only 8 bits wide (maximum value 255). To add numbers larger than 255, the CPU has to do multiple slow steps: add the lower byte, carry the 1, and add the upper byte.

[!NOTE] What is a Clock Cycle? - Microcontrollers have a quartz crystal oscillator that sends electrical pulses (clock ticks), say at 100 MHz (100 million ticks per second). - On each tick, the CPU does three basic steps: 1. Fetch: Electricity pulls instruction bits from Flash memory into the CPU. 2. Decode: Transistors figure out what the bits mean (e.g., 0001 means ADD). 3. Execute: The math unit runs the operation (e.g., adds Register R0 to R1). - Most simple instructions take just 1 clock cycle (one tick) to execute.

[!NOTE] What is ARM? - ARM is a company (ARM Ltd., based in the UK). - ARM does not manufacture physical silicon chips! They do not own chip factories (fabs). - Instead, ARM designs the CPU blueprints (the architecture and core circuits) and licenses them to chip manufacturers like STMicroelectronics (STM32), Raspberry Pi (RP2040/RP2350), NXP, and Apple. Those companies take ARM's blueprint, add peripherals (GPIO pins, timers, I2C, USB), and manufacture the real physical chips you buy.

docs.title: Decoding the Modular RISC-V Target (riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf)
docs.text:
While ARM dominates microcontrollers today, RISC-V (pronounced "risk-five") is the open-source architecture taking over the embedded industry (found in chips like the ESP32-C3, ESP32-C6, CH32v, and the dual ARM/RISC-V Raspberry Pi 2350).

Let's decode riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf: - riscv32 — 32-bit RISC-V architecture - imc — Hardware extension capabilities enabled on this chip - unknown — Hardware vendor - none — Bare metal (no OS, requires #![no_std]) - elf — Standard embedded binary format with debug symbols

docs.title: Modular ISA Extensions (I, M, A, C, F, D)
docs.text:
In RISC-V, chips are modular. Manufacturers pick only the hardware extensions they need: - I (Base Integer): The fundamental 32-bit integer instruction set (load, store, add, branch). Every RISC-V chip has this. - M (Hardware Integer Multiply & Divide): The chip has dedicated silicon circuits for integer multiplication and division. (Without M, multiplying two numbers requires dozens of slow addition loops in software). - A (Atomic Instructions): Hardware instructions for atomic memory operations (load-reserved, store-conditional, atomic swap/add). Essential for multi-core processors and lock-free concurrency. - C (Compressed Instructions): Enables 16-bit compressed instructions (identical in concept to ARM's Thumb mode). This reduces compiled binary size by 25%–30% to fit in tiny Flash storage. - F / D (Hardware Floating Point): Single (F, 32-bit f32) and Double (D, 64-bit f64) precision hardware Floating-Point Units (analogous to ARM's hf).

Target Architecture Common Example Chips thumbv7em-none-eabihf ARM Cortex-M4F / M7 STM32F4, STM32F7, nRF52840 riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf RISC-V 32-bit ESP32-C3, BL602 riscv32imac-unknown-none-elf RISC-V 32-bit (+ Atomic instructions) ESP32-C6, RP2350 (Hazard3 core)

[!TIP] Hardware Recommendation for Robotics - If we are building an IoT sensor node, home automation gadget, or simple WiFi-controlled robot: ESP32-C3 is cost-effective and capable. - If we are building a self-balancing robot, a drone flight controller, an inverse kinematics robot arm or running Kalman filters: pick a chip with hardware floating-point support (an ARM Cortex-M4F like STM32F4 / RP2040+FPU, or a RISC-V chip with F/D like the ESP32-S3 / ESP32-P4).

docs.title: Toolchain Management: rustup vs. Cargo
docs.text:
In Java, we manage JDKs and Maven/Gradle. In Python, we juggle python3, pyenv, and pip.

Rust unifies all of this under two tools: 1. rustup: Manages compiler versions and cross-compilation target modules. 2. Cargo: The package manager, dependency resolver, compiler orchestrator, and test runner.

docs.title: 1. Adding Target Architecture Support with rustup
docs.text:
When we install Rust, it only knows how to build binaries for our laptop (e.g., x86_64). To cross-compile for our robot, tell rustup to download the pre-compiled core library for our chip's architecture:

# Add ARM Cortex-M4F support:
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf

# Add RISC-V support:
rustup target add riscv32imc-unknown-none-elf

docs.title: 2. Cross-Compiling with Cargo
docs.text:
To compile our project for the microcontroller:

cargo build --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf

docs.title: Concept 1: What is a "Crate"? (Packages in Rust)
docs.text:
In Rust, a Crate is simply a package of code.

Language What it's called Where packages come from Python Module / package (e.g., requests, numpy) PyPI (pip install) Java Package / JAR library (e.g., commons-lang.jar) Maven Central (pom.xml) Rust Crate (e.g., heapless, embedded-hal) crates.io (Cargo.toml)

There are only two kinds of crates: 1. Binary Crate: Has a fn main() function. It compiles into a real runnable program or firmware file that we can flash to a chip. 2. Library Crate: Does not have a main() function. It is reusable helper code that we import into our project (like importing math in Python).

docs.title: Concept 2: Project Manifest vs. Workshop Config (Cargo.toml vs. .cargo/config.toml)
TOML Syntax Basics
docs.text:
• TOML stands for Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language.
  • Created by Tom Preston-Werner (co-founder of GitHub) as a cleaner alternative to YAML and JSON.
  • Key Features:
  • Natively supports comments (#), trailing commas, and explicit key-value pairs.
  • Does not rely on whitespace indentation for hierarchy.
Concept TOML Syntax Cargo Manifest Usage Key-Value Pairs name = "value" Setting metadata like name, version, and edition Tables (Sections) [section_name] Declaring namespaces such as [package] or [dependencies] Inline Tables crate = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] } Concise single-line dependency declarations with options Arrays members = ["crates/core", "crates/cli"] Declaring lists of features, authors, or workspace members

docs.title: Why Two Files? (The Workshop Analogy)
docs.text:
Think of your project like an engineering workshop:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      
│ 1. Cargo.toml (The Project Recipe)                                          │      
│    - What is my project called?                                             │      
│    - What version is it?                                                    │      
│    - What external crates (libraries) do I need?                            │      
│    - Equivalent to: pom.xml in Java, or requirements.txt in Python.         │      
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤      
│ 2. .cargo/config.toml (The Hardware & Workshop Settings)                    │      
│    - What physical chip am I building for right now?                        │      
│    - What command flashes the USB cable when I type `cargo run`?            │      
│    - What low-level memory maps should the linker use?                      │      
│    - Equivalent to: Compiler flags and IDE run configurations.              │      
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Where do they sit in our project folder?
docs.text:
my_drone_project/                                                                    
├── .cargo/                                                                          
│   └── config.toml      <-- Hardware & toolchain settings (target, runner, flags)   
├── src/                                                                             
│   └── main.rs          <-- Your actual Rust code                                   
└── Cargo.toml           <-- Project name & library dependencies

docs.title: Concept 3: Compiler Profiles & Binary Size Optimization (opt-level, LTO, codegen-units, panic="abort")
docs.text:
Microcontrollers have extremely limited Flash storage. By default, debug builds contain extra checks and unoptimized code that may not fit onto a 64 KB or 512 KB Flash chip.

In embedded Rust, we configure specific compiler flags in Cargo.toml to optimize binary size and remove unnecessary overhead:

[profile.dev]
# Level 1 optimization makes debug builds small enough to fit on the chip:
opt-level = 1

[profile.release]
# Optimize for binary size ("z" or "s") or speed (3):
opt-level = "s"
# Link-Time Optimization: removes dead functions across all crates:
lto = true
# Compile the entire project as 1 unit to maximize optimizations:
codegen-units = 1
# Remove stack unwinding tables; embedded crashes halt immediately:
panic = "abort"

Here is what each setting means: * opt-level (Optimization Level): * 0: Zero optimization. Compiles fast, but the binary is huge and slow (default on laptops). * 1 or 2: Medium optimization. Makes debug code small enough to fit on our chip while keeping debugging easy. * 3: Maximum speed (runs calculations as fast as possible). * "s": Optimize for Size. Makes the binary as few bytes as possible. * "z": Optimize for size aggressively (strips even more bytes). * lto = true (Link-Time Optimization): * Imagine packing a backpack for a hike. If you pack a giant Swiss Army knife but only need scissors, LTO cuts away the knife, saw, and bottle opener. It deletes any unused library function across all crates so it doesn't waste chip space. * codegen-units = 1: * Normally, the compiler splits our code into multiple chunks so laptop CPU cores can compile them in parallel. * Setting this to 1 forces the compiler to analyze all code as a single unit. It takes a few seconds longer to compile, but the compiler finds more opportunities to shrink the binary. * panic = "abort": * On a laptop, when a program crashes, it prints a 50-line "stack trace" showing which file and line caused the error. * Printing a stack trace requires hundreds of lines of string-formatting code that eats up Flash memory. A drone in mid-air has no screen anyway! * "abort" tells the chip: "If an error happens, just stop the CPU immediately. Do not waste memory storing crash-printing code."

docs.title: Concept 4: Low-Level Compiler Switches & Linker Scripts (rustflags & -Tlink.x)
docs.text:
Typing --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf on every single terminal command is tedious. In embedded projects, we automate this in .cargo/config.toml:

[build]
# Default compilation target (no need to pass --target in terminal):
target = "thumbv7em-none-eabihf"

[target.thumbv7em-none-eabihf]
# Instructs `cargo run` to directly flash the chip using probe-rs:
runner = "probe-rs run --chip STM32F401RE"

# Pass hardware-specific linker scripts:
rustflags = [
  "-C", "link-arg=-Tlink.x",
]
  • rustflags: Low-level command-line switches passed straight to the raw rustc compiler behind the scenes.
  • What is -C link-arg=-Tlink.x?
  • When we compile code on a laptop, the Linux or Windows operating system chooses where to load the program in RAM.
  • Microcontrollers have no operating system. The CPU needs a map of the physical silicon:
Physical Silicon Memory Map:
Flash Memory (Code)  : Starts at address 0x08000000 (Length: 512 KB)
RAM (Variables)      : Starts at address 0x20000000 (Length: 96 KB)
  • A Linker Script (often named link.x or memory.x) is that physical map.
  • -Tlink.x tells the compiler: "Look at this memory map file so you place instructions in physical Flash and variables in physical RAM!"

docs.title: Concept 5: Automated Hardware Flashing & Live Debugging (runner = "probe-rs run")
docs.text:
On our laptop, typing cargo run launches the program on our laptop's Intel/AMD processor.

But our compiled microcontroller firmware is written for ARM or RISC-V. Our laptop cannot run it directly.

The runner setting in .cargo/config.toml tells Cargo:

"Hey Cargo, when I type cargo run, don't run this binary on my laptop! Send it through the USB cable, flash it directly into the microcontroller's Flash memory, and stream its output back into my terminal!"

probe-rs is the modern, open-source tool that handles flashing and live debugging over USB.

docs.title: 1.3 Variables, Immutability by Default, and Shadowing
1. Immutability by Default (let)
docs.text:
When we create a variable using let, we are not creating a changeable container. We are creating a permanent binding between a name and a value.

fn main() {
    let target_altitude = 50; // In meters 

    // ERROR! The compiler refuses to compile this:
    target_altitude = 65;
}

If we try to change target_altitude, the Rust compiler stops us cold with an error.

docs.title: 2. Explicit Mutability (let mut)
docs.text:
What if a value needs to change—like current motor speed, battery percentage, or a loop counter?

We must explicitly ask the compiler for permission by adding the keyword mut (short for mutable):

fn main() {
    let mut current_rpm: u16 = 0;

    current_rpm = 1200; // Allowed!
    current_rpm = 1850; // Allowed!
}

docs.title: Why force you to type mut?
docs.text:
1. Human Clarity: When we read 500 lines of flight control code, our brain only has to track the variables marked mut. Everything else is guaranteed never to change behind our back.
  2. Compiler Optimization: When the compiler knows a value never changes, it can place it directly into a CPU hardware register or inline it into physical Flash storage, saving precious RAM.

[!TIP] NASA Power of 10 Rule #6 Connection Remember Rule 6 from our Power of 10: "Minimize Variable Scopes and Enforce Immutability."

Always start with plain let. Only add mut if you get a compiler error saying the variable must be modified.

[!NOTE] Loop Variables - In a standard for loop, we don't need mut for the loop counter itself (for i in 0..10). - We only need mut if we have an accumulator outside the loop or if we explicitly mutate an external variable inside the loop body.

docs.title: 3. Variable Shadowing: Rust's Secret Weapon
docs.text:
In Rust, we can declare a new variable with the exact same name as an older variable using the let keyword again:

fn main() {
    let sensor_pin = 4;

    // We "shadow" the old sensor_pin by declaring a new one with 'let':
    let sensor_pin = sensor_pin + 1;

    // sensor_pin is now 5!
}

At first glance, it looks like we are modifying a variable, then why not use let mut?

NO! Shadowing is completely different from mutation in two huge ways:

docs.title: Difference 1: We can change the Type (without losing type safety)
docs.text:
• First, the chip's ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) gives us a raw integer between 0 and 4095.
  • Then, we convert that integer into physical distance (a decimal float in centimeters: 15.4 cm).

With let mut, we cannot change types: 

let mut distance = 1024;  // distance is an integer (i32)
distance = 15.4;         // ❌ ERROR! Rust says: "Expected integer, found float"

With Shadowing, we can safely transform types: 

let distance = 1024;              // 1. Raw integer reading from hardware
let distance = distance as f32;  // 2. Convert to float
let distance = distance * 0.05; // 3. Calibrated distance in cm: 51.2 cm

More idiomatic Rust form using distinct, descriptive names: 

let raw_adc: u16 = 1024;
let distance_cm: f32 = (raw_adc as f32) * 0.05;

docs.title: Difference 2: The result is frozen (Immutable) again!
docs.text:
Notice that every step uses plain let (not let mut). * During the calculation, you shadow the intermediate value. * Once the math is done, distance is completely immutable. * No other function or line of code can accidentally corrupt distance later!

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                  
│ SHADOWING VS. MUTATION: THE EMBEDDED PERSPECTIVE                            │                  
│                                                                             │                  
│ 1. MUTATION (`let mut x`):                                                  │                  
│    [Same RAM slot] ───> Overwrite value (Type CANNOT change)                │                  
│    Risk: Stays changeable forever throughout the entire function.           │                  
│                                                                             │                  
│ 2. SHADOWING (`let x ... let x`):                                           │                  
│    [Old variable]  ───> Hidden / Dropped by compiler                        │                  
│    [New variable]  ───> Fresh binding (Type CAN change! Can be immutable!)  │                  
│    Safety: Transforms data step-by-step, then locks it down cold.           │                   
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 4. Constants (const) vs. Immutable Variables (let)
docs.text:
Beginners often ask: "If let x = 5; cannot change, why does Rust also have const X: u32 = 5;?"

Here is the fundamental difference:

Feature let x = 5; (Immutable Variable) const X: u32 = 5; (Compile-Time Constant) When it runs Evaluated at Runtime when that line executes Computed at Compile-Time by rustc Type Annotation Optional (Rust infers it automatically) Mandatory (you must write : u32) Where it can live Only inside functions or blocks { } Anywhere (including global module scope) RAM Usage Uses a stack slot or CPU register Zero RAM! Inlined directly into Flash memory Naming Convention snake_case UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

docs.title: Practical Robotics Example:
docs.text:
const SYSTEM_CLOCK_HZ: u32 = 168_000_000; // 168 MHz (STM32F4)
const MAX_STEERING_ANGLE_DEG: f32 = 45.0;

fn calculate_pwm(duty_cycle: f32) {
    // Runtime immutable variable (computed dynamically from sensor):
    let current_voltage = read_battery_voltage();
}

[!TIP] Number Readability in Rust Notice the underscore in 168_000_000? In Rust, we can place underscores anywhere inside numeric literals to make them easy to read, just like commas in English (168,000,000). The compiler simply ignores them!

docs.title: Deep Dive: Two Silicon Rules for const vs. let
Rule 1: const physically cannot use runtime data
docs.text:
A const value must be 100% known to the compiler while sitting on your host laptop during compilation:

// ❌ This will not compile: sensor values do not exist at compile-time!
const CURRENT_TEMP: f32 = read_temperature_sensor();

// ✅ Must use `let`:
let current_temp: f32 = read_temperature_sensor();

Any value that comes from: - A sensor reading - An ADC voltage conversion - A function parameter (fn drive(speed: u8)) - Hardware timers or clocks

... cannot be a const. They must be let.

docs.title: Rule 2: The compiler optimizes let with Constant Folding (Zero-Cost Abstraction)
docs.text:
In release mode (cargo build --release), the LLVM optimizer runs an optimization called Constant Folding & Propagation:

fn calculate_motor_speed() {
    let base_speed = 50;
    let boost = 10;
    let final_speed = base_speed + boost;
    set_motor(final_speed);
}

Even though we used let, the compiler is smart enough to realize base_speed and boost never change. It computes 50 + 10 = 60 during compilation on your laptop and translates the whole function into:

set_motor(60); // Uses zero RAM! Directly hardcoded by optimizer

docs.title: The Golden Rule: Which One to Use?
docs.text: Use const for: Use let (immutable) for: 1. Hardware Pin Definitions (const MOTOR_PWM_PIN: u8 = 9;) 1. All local calculations & algorithm steps 2. Physics & System Constants (const MAX_RPM: u32 = 6000;) 2. Function parameters and return values 3. Buffer Dimensions (const RX_BUF_SIZE: usize = 64;) 3. Intermediate sensor & data transformation steps

docs.title: 5. Variable Scope and Block Expressions
docs.text:
In Rust, curly brackets { ... } create a lexical scope.

Variables created inside a block die immediately when the closing bracket } is reached. Their memory is instantly reclaimed:

fn main() {
    let main_motor = 1;

    {
        let temporary_boost = 50;
        println!("Boost active: {}", temporary_boost);
    } // <-- `temporary_boost` DIES right here!

    // ❌ ERROR! temporary_boost no longer exists:
    // println!("{}", temporary_boost);
}

docs.title: Expression Blocks (Returning Values from {})
docs.text:
In Python and Java, {} is just a syntax container for statements.

In Rust, a block is an expression that can return a value!

If you omit the semicolon on the last line of the block, that line becomes the return value of the entire block:

fn main() {
    let motor_rpm = {
        let battery_voltage = 11.1;   // 3S LiPo battery
        let motor_kv = 920.0;         // Drone motor rating

        battery_voltage * motor_kv    // <-- NO semicolon! This is returned!
    };

    // `motor_rpm` is now 10212.0!
    // And best of all: `battery_voltage` and `motor_kv` are already deleted
    // from memory! Zero wasted RAM on our microcontroller!
}

docs.title: 6. Language Paradigm Comparison: Python vs. Java vs. Rust
docs.text: Feature Python Java Rust Default Behavior Mutable (x = 5; x = 10) Mutable (int x = 5;) Immutable (let x = 5;) To Make Changeable Always changeable Changeable by default Must write let mut To Make Permanent Not enforced (only conventions like PI = 3.14) Write final int x = 5; Default (let x = 5;) or const Shadowing in Same Scope Allowed, but changes type dynamically at runtime Illegal (compiler error: duplicate variable) Fully Supported with compile-time safety Block Returns Value No No Yes (let x = { ... val };)

docs.title: 7. Real-World Case Study: How Physical Reality Becomes Rust Numbers (The ADC & Sensor Signal Chain)
docs.text:
When building robots and drones, how does a real physical obstacle in the world turn into a software number like 15.4 cm?

Microcontrollers cannot read real-world continuous signals directly—the CPU only understands binary bits (0 and 1).

Here is the complete journey of how an obstacle in front of your robot becomes a usable number in Rust:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HOW PHYSICAL REALITY BECOMES RUST NUMBERS (THE SENSOR SIGNAL CHAIN)         │
│                                                                             │
│ 1. Physical World : Obstacle is placed 15.4 cm in front of the robot.       │
│                               │                                             │
│                               ▼                                             │
│ 2. Analog Sensor  : Infrared detector outputs an analog voltage (1.54 V).   │
│                               │                                             │
│                               ▼                                             │
│ 3. 12-Bit ADC     : Microcontroller slices 0 V – 3.3 V into 0 – 4095.       │
│                     (1.54 V / 3.3 V) * 4095 = Raw Integer 1912              │
│                               │                                             │
│                               ▼                                             │
│ 4. Rust Firmware  : Math formula converts 1912 -> 1.54 V -> 15.4 cm.        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Step A: Where does 4095 come from? (The 12-Bit ADC)
docs.text:
The silicon hardware block inside your chip that measures analog voltage is called an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter).

Most modern microcontrollers (such as the STM32, ESP32, and RP2040) have a 12-bit ADC: * A 1-bit ADC can only count \(2^1 = 2\) values: 0 or 1. * An 8-bit ADC (used in older chips like the Arduino Uno) can count \(2^8 = 256\) values: 0 to 255. * A 12-bit ADC has 12 binary switches: \(2^{12} = 4096\) possible discrete steps. * Because digital systems count starting from 0, the integer range is 0 to 4095 (\(4096 - 1\)).

docs.title: How the ADC Slices Voltage
docs.text:
Your microcontroller typically runs on 3.3 V. The 12-bit ADC chops that 3.3 V range into 4,095 equal electrical slices:

Physical Voltage on Pin Raw ADC Integer Read by Rust (u16) Electrical Meaning 0.0 V 0 Ground (No voltage) 1.65 V 2047 Halfway voltage 3.3 V 4095 Maximum operating voltage

docs.title: Step B: Where does 15.4 cm come from? (The Sensor Calibration Math)
docs.text:
Suppose your robot uses an analog infrared distance sensor (e.g., an optical distance sensor):

  1. Light Reflection: When an obstacle is 15.4 cm away, the sensor's optical receiver outputs an analog signal of 1.54 V.
  2. Pin Input: That voltage enters an ADC-capable GPIO pin on your chip.
  3. Silicon Quantization: The 12-bit ADC converts 1.54 V into an integer: $\(\text{Raw Integer} = \frac{1.54\text{ V}}{3.3\text{ V}} \times 4095 \approx 1912\)$
  4. Firmware Math: In your Rust code, you read the integer 1912 and convert it back into voltage, then into physical centimeters using the sensor manufacturer's datasheet formula:
// 1. Read raw ADC integer from the hardware pin:
let raw_adc: u16 = adc.read_pin(); // e.g., 1912

// 2. Convert raw integer (0..4095) into physical voltage:
let voltage: f32 = (raw_adc as f32 / 4095.0) * 3.3; // 1.54 V

// 3. Sensor datasheet formula: converts Voltage -> Centimeters:
let distance_cm: f32 = voltage * 10.0; // 15.4 cm!

[!TIP] Why Variable Shadowing Fits Here Notice how the measurement transforms step-by-step: raw ADC integer (u16) \(\rightarrow\) voltage (f32) \(\rightarrow\) final distance (f32). This is where Rust's variable shadowing or distinct variable naming shines: intermediate raw values are processed, and the final physical measurement is locked down as an immutable value.

docs.title: 8. Explicit Type Annotations vs. Type Inference (let x: u32 = 5; vs. let x = 5;)
docs.text:
In Rust, you can declare variables with or without explicit types:

let x: u32 = 5; // Explicit type annotation
let x = 5;      // Type inference (compiler figures it out)

docs.title: Does this affect machine code or runtime speed?
docs.text:
NO. Both forms produce the exact same machine code.

At runtime on the physical microcontroller: * Both versions execute at the exact same clock cycle speed. * Both take up the exact same number of bytes in memory. * There is zero performance penalty.

Rust's type deduction is purely a compile-time convenience performed on your development PC before generating the binary.

docs.title: The 3 Critical Traps in Embedded Programming
docs.text: While desktop developers can rely heavily on type inference, embedded developers must be aware of three critical traps:

docs.title: Trap 1: The Hidden Float Trap (f64 vs. f32) ⚠️ (CRITICAL FOR ROBOTICS)
docs.text:
If you write a decimal number without specifying a type: 

let speed = 15.4; // Rust defaults this to f64 (64-bit double precision)!

  • Why this is dangerous on microcontrollers:
  • Most robotics microcontrollers (like the ARM Cortex-M4F or Cortex-M7) only have a 32-bit hardware FPU (f32). They do not have physical hardware circuits for 64-bit f64 math.
  • If you leave a decimal as f64, the compiler is forced to inject hundreds of instructions of software math emulation, making your motor and sensor control loops up to 50× slower!
  • The Embedded Fix: Always explicitly specify f32 for decimals: 
    let speed: f32 = 15.4;
// OR use a type suffix:
let speed = 15.4f32;

docs.title: Trap 2: The Hidden Integer Trap (i32 default)
docs.text:
If you write a whole number without specifying a type: 

let pin_number = 13; // Rust defaults this to i32 (signed 32-bit integer)!

  • Why this causes compile errors:
  • Microcontroller pin numbers, peripheral register bitmasks, and byte buffers almost always expect an unsigned 8-bit integer (u8).
  • If you pass pin_number (i32) into a hardware driver expecting u8, the compiler stops you because a signed 32-bit integer cannot safely fit into an 8-bit unsigned slot.
  • The Embedded Fix: 
    let pin_number: u8 = 13;
// OR use a type suffix:
let pin_number = 13u8;

docs.title: Trap 3: The "Cannot Infer Type" Compiler Ambiguity
docs.text:
Sometimes the compiler cannot deduce your intended type because multiple types are valid. A classic example is string parsing: 

// ❌ Compilation Error: "cannot infer type"
// The compiler doesn't know whether to parse into u8, u16, u32, or i32:
let sensor_id = "42".parse().unwrap();

// ✅ Solution: Provide an explicit type hint:
let sensor_id: u8 = "42".parse().unwrap();

docs.title: Practical Rule of Thumb for Embedded Rust
docs.text: Situation What to Write Engineering Reason Normal local calculations let total = count * 2; Clean and readable. Rust infers the type directly from count. Decimals on microcontrollers let dist: f32 = 15.4;(or 15.4f32) Prevents the slow f64 software-emulation trap. Guarantees single-cycle hardware FPU execution. Hardware pins & byte buffers let pin: u8 = 5;(or 5u8) Microcontroller registers require exact bit-widths (u8, u16, u32). Ambiguous function calls let val: u32 = ...; Resolves compiler ambiguity when multiple types implement the same method.

docs.title: 9. Deferred Initialization: Zero Garbage Memory (Definite Assignment Analysis)
docs.text:
In older languages like C and C++, you can declare a variable without giving it a value:

// Dangerous C code on a microcontroller:
int sensor_val; // UNINITIALIZED!

if (mode == FAST_MODE) {
    sensor_val = read_fast_sensor();
}
// BUG: What if mode is SLOW_MODE?
// `sensor_val` still holds whatever random electrical garbage was left in RAM!
send_motor_pwm(sensor_val); // Motors might spin violently!

In microcontrollers, RAM chips power on with random 1s and 0s left over from stray capacitance. Reading an uninitialized variable in C means you are operating on random electrical noise.

docs.title: How Rust Solves This Safely
docs.text:
In Rust, you are allowed to declare a variable before assigning it, but the compiler enforces Definite Assignment Analysis:

let sensor_val: u16; // 1. Declared with an explicit type, but unassigned

if emergency_stop {
    sensor_val = 0;
} else {
    sensor_val = adc.read_pin();
}

// 2. Safe to use! The compiler PROVES that every single branch gave it a value:
set_motor_speed(sensor_val);

docs.title: What happens if you forget an execution branch?
docs.text:
If you forget the else branch:

let sensor_val: u16;

if emergency_stop {
    sensor_val = 0;
}

// ❌ COMPILER ERROR:
// Rust stops the build: "used binding `sensor_val` isn't initialized"
set_motor_speed(sensor_val);

[!NOTE] Idiomatic Alternative: if as an Expression While deferred initialization is 100% safe in Rust, an even cleaner way is to use if as an expression directly: 

let sensor_val: u16 = if emergency_stop {
    0
} else {
    adc.read_pin()
};
This binds and initializes the variable in a single step with zero ambiguity.

docs.title: 10. The Three Storage Classes in Silicon: let vs. const vs. static
docs.text:
When you write firmware, every byte lives in one of three places in physical silicon:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ HOW RUST VARIABLES LIVE IN MICROCONTROLLER SILICON                          │
│                                                                             │
│ 1. `let x = 5;`        ──> STACK / CPU REGISTERS                            │
│                            • Created dynamically when function runs.        │
│                            • Instantly reclaimed when function exits.       │
│                            • Zero heap memory used.                         │
│                                                                             │
│ 2. `const X: u32 = 5;` ──> INLINED INTO FLASH INSTRUCTIONS (NO MEMORY SLOT) │
│                            • Replaced at compile-time by literal numbers.   │
│                            • Assembly: `MOV R0, #5`                         │
│                            • Has NO physical RAM address!                   │
│                                                                             │
│ 3. `static X: u32 = 5;`──> FIXED PERMANENT SILICON ADDRESS (FLASH or RAM)   │
│                            • Stays at the exact same memory address         │
│                              from power-on until the battery dies.          │
│                            • Placed in `.rodata` (Flash) or `.data` (RAM).  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Detailed Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature let (Local Variable) const (Compile-Time Constant) static (Global Storage) Physical Memory Location Stack (RAM) or CPU Registers (R0–R12) None (Inlined into CPU instructions in Flash) Permanent address in Flash (.rodata) or RAM (.data/.bss) Memory Address Temporary address on the stack Has no memory address Permanent fixed memory address Lifespan Dies when enclosing block { } ends Lives forever (inlined into code) Lives forever (from boot to shutdown) Evaluation Time Runtime Compile-time Compile-time initialization Type Annotation Optional (inferred) Mandatory Mandatory Primary Use in Robotics Local calculations & algorithm steps Pin numbers, calibration factors, physics math Global hardware buffers (DMA queues, UART buffers), shared interrupt state

docs.title: Sneak Peek: Decoding an Embedded static Buffer
docs.text:
static UART_RX_BUFFER: [u8; 128] = [0; 128];
// │         │              │            │  
// │         │              │            └─ VALUE: "Repeat the number 0, exactly 128 times"
// │         │              └────────────── DATA_TYPE: "A fixed array of 128 bytes"
// │         └───────────────────────────── NAME: Variable name (UPPERCASE because it's static)
// └─────────────────────────────────────── KEYWORD: Permanent fixed address in memory

docs.title: 1. What does [u8; 128] mean? (The Data Type)
docs.text:
In Python, a list [1, 2, 3] can grow or shrink whenever you call .append(). That requires a dynamic heap memory allocator (which we banned under NASA Rule #3).

In Bare-Metal Embedded Rust, arrays must have a fixed, unchangeable size known at compile time:

\[\text{[ Type ; How many ]}\]
  • [u8; 4] means: An array of exactly 4 bytes (e.g., [10, 20, 30, 40]).
  • [u8; 128] means: An array of exactly 128 bytes (u8), sitting side-by-side in physical RAM.

docs.title: 2. What does [0; 128] mean? (The Value)
docs.text:
If you need an array with 128 zeros, typing:

[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, ... /* 128 times! */]

would be painful and messy.

Rust gives you a shortcut syntax to fill an array with repeating values:

\[\text{[ Value to repeat ; How many times ]}\]
  • [0; 128] tells the compiler: "Fill all 128 slots with the number 0."
  • [255; 4] produces: [255, 255, 255, 255].

docs.title: 3. Why is it used with static? (The Hardware Story)
docs.text:
In robotics, UART (Serial) is the hardware communication wire that connects your microcontroller to a GPS module, Bluetooth, or your PC.

[!NOTE] What is UART? (The Robot's Voice & Ears) UART stands for Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter. It is the simplest and most fundamental serial communication protocol in hardware: * TX (Transmit Pin): The pin the microcontroller uses to speak (send bytes out). * RX (Receive Pin): The pin the microcontroller uses to listen (receive bytes in). * GND (Ground Pin): The shared electrical ground reference.

┌───────────────────────────┐                 ┌───────────────────────────┐
│ Microcontroller (Robot)   │    TX Wire      │ Your Laptop / GPS Sensor  │
│   [ TX (Transmit) Pin ]   │ ──────────────> │   [ RX (Receive) Pin ]    │
│                           │    RX Wire      │                           │
│   [ RX (Receive) Pin  ]   │ <────────────── │   [ TX (Transmit) Pin ]   │
│   [ GND (Ground) Pin  ]   │ ─────────────── │   [ GND (Ground) Pin  ]   │
└───────────────────────────┘                 └───────────────────────────┘
Whenever you connect your robot to your laptop over USB to stream debug telemetry or wire a GPS / Bluetooth module to your board, you are using UART to exchange bytes!

When the GPS sends data, characters arrive byte-by-byte into the chip.

  • The microcontroller needs a permanent parking lot in RAM to store those incoming bytes until your code is ready to read them.
  • That parking lot is called a Buffer.
  • Because the serial hardware runs continuously in the background (even while your main code is doing motor calculations), this buffer cannot be a temporary local variable inside a function (let) that dies when the function ends.
  • It must sit at a permanent, fixed address in physical RAM from power-on until the battery dies. That is why it is marked static!
Physical Microcontroller RAM:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 0x20000000: UART_RX_BUFFER (128 bytes reserved for GPS)     │
│ [ 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | ... 128 zeroed byte slots ... | 0 ]   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 1.4 Primitive Types: Fixed-width Integers, Floats, Booleans, and Chars
docs.text:
In high-level languages like Python or JavaScript, you rarely think about how many bits a number occupies in physical silicon. You write x = 100 or let x = 100, and the runtime engine handles memory allocation behind the scenes.

In Bare-Metal Embedded Rust, every single bit matters. When you configure a hardware timer, read an ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter), or toggle an LED on a microcontroller, your code directly manipulates physical registers. Selecting the wrong type can cause silent bugs, data corruption, or catastrophic failures.

docs.title: 1. Fixed-Width Integers: Why Embedded C Got It Wrong
docs.text:
In C, the size of basic types like int or long is implementation-defined: * On an 8-bit AVR microcontroller (e.g., Arduino Uno), int is 16 bits (2 bytes). * On a 32-bit ARM Cortex-M microcontroller (e.g., STM32), int is 32 bits (4 bytes). * On a 64-bit x86/x64 PC, long might be 32 bits or 64 bits depending on the operating system.

This ambiguity has historically caused severe bugs when porting software between microcontrollers.

Rust eliminates integer ambiguity. Every integer type explicitly declares its signedness and exact bit width:

 ┌─────────────────── Unsigned (Zero or Positive only: 0 to 2ⁿ - 1)
 │    ┌────────────── Signed Two's Complement (-2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ - 1)
 ▼    ▼
 u8   i8   ───  8 bits  (1 byte)
u16  i16   ─── 16 bits  (2 bytes)
u32  i32   ─── 32 bits  (4 bytes)
u64  i64   ─── 64 bits  (8 bytes)
u128 i128  ─── 128 bits (16 bytes)
usize isize ── Pointer-sized (32 bits on Cortex-M, 64 bits on x86_64)

Physical Memory Footprint Comparison:
┌──────────┬────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Type     │ Size in Hardware RAM   │ Valid Numeric Range                     │
├──────────┼────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ u8       │ 1 Byte  (8 bits)       │ 0 to 255                                │
│ i8       │ 1 Byte  (8 bits)       │ -128 to +127                            │
│ u16      │ 2 Bytes (16 bits)      │ 0 to 65,535                             │
│ i16      │ 2 Bytes (16 bits)      │ -32,768 to +32,767                      │
│ u32      │ 4 Bytes (32 bits)      │ 0 to 4,294,967,295                      │
│ i32      │ 4 Bytes (32 bits)      │ -2,147,483,648 to +2,147,483,647        │
│ u64      │ 8 Bytes (64 bits)      │ 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615         │
│ usize    │ Target architecture    │ 32-bit (0..4.29B) or 64-bit             │
└──────────┴────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 2. Hardware Mapping: Which Type to Use in Robotics?
docs.text:
In firmware and robotics, choose integer types based on physical hardware interfaces:

  1. u8 (The Byte Worker):
  2. Use Cases: Serial communication bytes (UART, SPI, I2C), 8-bit PWM motor duty cycle (0 = stopped, 255 = 100% full throttle), color channels (RGB 0..255).

  3. Why Unsigned? A byte received over a radio link or GPS cannot be negative.

  4. u16 (The Sensor & Timer Specialist):

  5. Use Cases: Microcontroller ADC readings (typical microcontrollers feature 10-bit or 12-bit ADCs yielding values from 0 to 4095), 16-bit hardware timer reload values (ARR).

  6. u32 (The Architectural Standard):

  7. Use Cases: Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers (GPIOx_ODR, RCC_CR), 32-bit hardware timers, physical memory addresses.

  8. Note: On 32-bit ARM Cortex-M processors, u32 is native. Operations on u32 execute in a single CPU clock cycle.

  9. i16 / i32 (Sensors with Direction):

  10. Use Cases: 3-axis Accelerometer and Gyroscope (IMU) readings. Forward acceleration is positive, backward acceleration is negative. Temperature sensors reading below \(0^\circ\text{C}\).

  11. usize / isize (Memory Offsets and Indices):

  12. Rule: In Rust, arrays and slices can only be indexed using usize.
  13. On a 32-bit microcontroller (like STM32), usize is automatically 32 bits. On your 64-bit PC, it is automatically 64 bits.
// Embedded Example: Practical Variable Declarations
let motor_pwm: u8 = 180;             // Motor speed: 180 / 255 (~70% duty cycle)
let raw_adc: u16 = 3120;             // 12-bit ADC reading (range: 0 to 4095)
